catalog_entry.label: Knockout tie method of victory/finish
catalog_entry.target: Whether a knockout tie (or a named team's win) is decided in regulation, extra time, or a penalty shootout.
catalog_entry.mechanism: A single-match knockout final is decided in one of three ordered phases. Regulation (90 minutes plus stoppage) ends the tie when the score is unequal; otherwise 30 minutes of extra time are played, and a level score after 120 minutes goes to a penalty shootout. Method of Finish asks which phase ends the tie; Method of Victory asks which phase a named team wins in. The probability mass is generated by the regulation-draw probability (driven by the strength gap, the low total goal rate typical of finals and late risk aversion), the extra-time scoring rate under fatigue and extra substitutions, and a near-coin-flip shootout.

Share of level-at-90 outcomes settled before a shootout.

interactions.hypothesis: A small strength gap combined with a cagey final multiplies the regulation-draw probability, so the ET and penalty phases gain most when both conditions hold.
Extra-time goals come disproportionately from the side with fresher, better substitutes, so depth shifts both the ET-versus-penalties split and who wins in ET.
A side that rates its shootout chances better is more willing to play for penalties, raising the level-at-120 probability.

contract.settlement_definition: Binary markets per phase on one knockout final. MOF (KXUCLMOF, KXWCMOF) settles YES for the phase in which either team wins the trophy/advances; MOV (KXUELMOV, KXWCMOV) settles YES only if the named team wins in that phase. Regular/Regulation Time includes the 90 minutes plus all stoppage time and excludes extra time and the shootout; Extra Time is a win after extra time but before any shootout; Penalty Shootout is a win via shootout after regulation and extra time. Cancellation or rescheduling more than two weeks away resolves to a fair price. The source of truth is not named in the sampled text.

Stoppage time at the end of 90 minutes counts as Regular Time; a goal at 90+8 is regulation, while a goal at 91' of extra time is Extra Time.
An abandoned final replayed within two weeks presumably settles on the replay; beyond two weeks a fair price applies, and the fair-price method is truncated in the sampled text.

mechanism.summary: The outcome is the phase that breaks the tie in a single match. First, the two finalists' attack and defence strengths, adjusted for opponent quality and neutral venue, give regulation goal rates; finals run below league rates and draw more often, so the regulation-level probability is typically around 25-35% when the sides are close. Second, low-score dependence and late conservatism at level scores fatten the 0-0/1-1 cells. Third, conditional on level at 90, extra time runs at a reduced, fatigue- and substitute-dependent rate, so roughly half or more of level matches stay level to 120. Fourth, the shootout is close to a coin flip with small skill and goalkeeper effects. MOV multiplies each phase probability by the team's share of that phase. Settlement wording decides stoppage-time allocation and the fair-price rule for cancellations.

stages.name: Regulation goal rates for a neutral-venue final
stages.description: Each finalist's expected goals in 90 minutes come from opponent-adjusted xG ratings shrunk to a long-memory rating, corrected for the confirmed XI and known absences. Home advantage is set to the small neutral-venue tilt from ticket share and travel rather than a league value. The knockout final multiplier lowers both rates, which matters because the level probability rises steeply as total goals fall.
stages.distribution: Bivariate goal counts with two Poisson-like rates; strength-gap uncertainty is approximately normal on the log-rate scale.

stages.name: Probability the final is level after 90 plus stoppage
stages.description: The regulation-level probability is the sum of diagonal cells of the score grid. Dixon-Coles dependence raises 0-0 and 1-1, the final-stage cagey factor raises draws further, and late risk aversion in the 75-90+ window at level scores reduces the decisive-goal hazard. This cell is the complement of MOF Regular Time YES and the shared base of all ET and penalty legs.
stages.distribution: A single probability near 0.2-0.4, concave in the strength gap (peaks when sides are equal) and decreasing in total goal rate.

stages.name: Extra-time resolution
stages.description: Given level at 90, 30 more minutes are played with an additional substitution allowance. Goal intensity is below a pro-rata share of the regulation rate because of fatigue and caution, and it tilts toward the side with the stronger bench and fewer cards. The phase decides how level-at-90 mass splits between Extra Time and Penalty Shootout legs and which team wins the Extra Time MOV leg.
stages.distribution: Goals in 30 minutes are low counts (mean roughly 0.5-0.8 combined); P(level at 120 | level at 90) is often 0.5-0.6.

stages.name: Penalty shootout
stages.description: Five alternating kicks per side then sudden death. Conversion is around 70-80% per kick, team skill differences are small and noisy, and first-kicker advantage is disputed in the literature. Goalkeeper save ability and the designated takers still on the pitch after 120 minutes are the only material inputs; heavy shrinkage toward 50% is required.
stages.distribution: Bernoulli winner with p close to 0.5; length is a stopping time but only the winner matters here.

stages.name: Contract phase mapping and settlement
stages.description: Regulation includes stoppage time, Extra Time ends before the shootout, and Penalty Shootout requires both earlier phases completed. MOF legs are either-team; MOV legs are team-specific. Trophy wording (UCL/UEL) versus advancement wording (World Cup) and a fair-price rule for cancellation beyond two weeks define the edge cases; no data source is named.
stages.distribution: Deterministic mapping from the phase and winner to six MOV or three MOF YES outcomes; fair-price settlements are rare continuous values.

soc.extra_time_phase_scoring_rate.label: Extra-time scoring rate conditional on reaching 90 minutes level
soc.extra_time_phase_scoring_rate.mechanism: Goal intensity in the 30 extra minutes differs from a pro-rata share of the 90-minute rate: legs are tired, a further substitution window opens, and both sides often trade risk for the shootout.
soc.extra_time_phase_scoring_rate.rationale: MOF/MOV contracts split level-at-90 mass between ET and penalties, so the ET rate (not the regulation rate) decides how much of that mass ends before a shootout. Pro-rating lambda_90 by 30/90 overstates ET goals in finals; the subtle part is that the discount depends on remaining substitutes and bench quality, which differ between the two sides.
soc.extra_time_phase_scoring_rate.measurement: From all knockout matches that went to extra time in UCL/UEL/UECL, World Cup, Euros, Copa America and top domestic cups since 2010: ET goals per 30 min divided by (model lambda_90 x 30/90) for the same match, fitted as a ratio with covariates (subs remaining at 90', bench xG-value per 90, red cards, final vs earlier round); shrink competition effects to the pooled ratio with k=40 matches; output per-team ET lambda as of the confirmed XI (T-60).
soc.extra_time_phase_scoring_rate.why: Decides what share of level-at-90 outcomes is settled in Extra Time rather than by Penalty Shootout.

soc.late_level_risk_appetite.label: Late-regulation risk appetite when a knockout match is level
soc.late_level_risk_appetite.mechanism: In the last 15 minutes of a level single-match knockout, one or both teams often lower attacking intensity and accept extra time, so the hazard of a decisive goal falls below the in-play baseline.
soc.late_level_risk_appetite.rationale: The probability the match is level at 90 is not a pure function of team goal rates: if both teams slow down at 1-1 after 75', the regulation-draw cell is inflated relative to Poisson/Dixon-Coles even after the stage-level cagey factor. The effect is asymmetric: a weaker side or a side with a better shootout record has more reason to play for ET.
soc.late_level_risk_appetite.measurement: Event-level: goals and shots per minute in minutes 75-90+stoppage when the score is level in single-match knockouts versus level league matches with the same pre-match rating gap; ratio estimated by competition tier with team random effect, shrink to pooled ratio with k=60 matches; split by pre-match underdog/favourite and by remaining substitutes; as-of = pre-match.
raw_data: shot and goal events with minute and score state
soc.late_level_risk_appetite.why: Inflates the Regular Time NO mass beyond what goal rates alone imply.

soc.neutral_final_venue_split.label: Neutral-venue final: crowd share, travel and pitch familiarity split
soc.neutral_final_venue_split.mechanism: Finals are played at pre-assigned neutral stadiums, so the usual home advantage is replaced by a partial advantage from ticket allocation, travel distance, climate and pitch familiarity.
soc.neutral_final_venue_split.rationale: Using league home advantage for a final mis-sets the strength gap and therefore the regulation-win versus level split. Allocation is often equal by rule, but secondary-market tickets, diaspora (e.g. World Cup matches in North America) and travel distance tilt it. The tilt is small; the risk is over-applying it.
soc.neutral_final_venue_split.measurement: For each final: share of attendance supporting each side (proxy: official allocation + estimated secondary share from local diaspora and distance), great-circle distance from each club/country base, kickoff local time vs body clock (hours), and whether either side has played at the stadium in the past 24 months; convert to a goal-rate offset by regressing goal difference residuals on these in neutral-venue finals since 2000 with heavy shrinkage toward zero (prior sd 0.05 goals).
soc.neutral_final_venue_split.why: Neutral-venue adjustment replaces league home advantage when splitting regulation outcomes in finals.

nonlinearities.shape: inverted-U (level probability peaks at zero strength gap)
nonlinearities.why: The regulation-draw probability is maximal for evenly matched finalists and falls on both sides as the gap grows, so MOF Regular Time NO is a concave function of the gap.

nonlinearities.shape: convex increase of level probability as total goal rate falls
nonlinearities.why: With total expected goals below about 2, the 0-0 and 1-1 cells grow faster than linearly, so a modest cagey multiplier moves the ET/penalty legs a lot.
Even large observed skill differences translate into only a few points of shootout win probability because kick conversion noise dominates small samples.

catalog_entry.label: Soccer same-match combination (parlay)
catalog_entry.target: Two or more match events in one game must all occur (e.g. a named player scores first and his team advances).
catalog_entry.mechanism: A prepack settles YES only if every leg occurs in the same match. The legs share one score path: for the sampled contract the player must score the first goal of the match at any point up to the end of extra time, and his team must then advance, which includes winning on penalties. The joint probability is the probability the player's team scores first times the player's share of that first goal (driven by minutes on the pitch, shot share and penalty duty), times the probability that a team leading first goes on to advance, which is high in knockouts but not certain because extra time and shootouts remain.

Start, substitute and DNP probabilities determine whether the player can score first at all.

How often the side that conceded first equalises, which breaks the advancement leg.
Team strengths set both who scores first and who advances.
Confirmed lineups move team rates and confirm the player's start.
Opponent's concession by route (set piece, penalty, own goal) shifts the player's share and the own-goal risk.
Leg wording differs per prepack and must be parsed each time.
Joint simulation gives P(advance | player scored first), the dependence that marginals miss.

interactions.hypothesis: If the player's first goals come early, his team has longer to lose the lead, so the conditional advancement leg is weaker than for late first goals.
A planned substitution of the player before the typical first-goal minute in a low-scoring match sharply cuts the scorer leg without changing the advancement leg.
The stronger the player's team, the smaller the uplift from scoring first because it would usually advance anyway; underdogs gain the most conditional uplift.

Advancement presumably includes a shootout win; a 0-0 after 120 minutes leaves no first goalscorer so the scorer leg fails. Treatment of own goals as the first goal, of Messi not playing, of postponement and the source of truth is not stated (rules_secondary is empty).

mechanism.summary: The sampled combo is a conjunction of two dependent events on one score path. First, the match must produce at least one goal within 120 minutes and the player's team must score it; this depends on the two teams' goal hazards. Second, the player must be on the pitch and be the scorer of that goal, which depends on his start probability, substitution timing, share of team shots and xG, and penalty duty. Third, conditional on his team leading first at minute t, it must advance: the lead must be held or restored, and if equalised, the match is decided in extra time or a shootout. The joint probability is therefore not the product of the legs' marginals; it is the integral over the first-goal minute of the scorer hazard times the conditional advancement probability at that minute. Contract parsing determines which goals and which advancement routes count.

stages.name: Which team scores the first goal and when
stages.description: Team goal hazards for Argentina and Switzerland, set from opponent-adjusted ratings and the confirmed XI, decide the probability that Argentina scores first, that Switzerland does, or that the match stays goalless for 120 minutes. The timing of the first goal is roughly exponential with a rate that rises slightly through each half; in a cagey knockout the goalless share is material.
stages.distribution: Competing risks over minutes with a point mass on no goal by 120 minutes (several percent in tight knockouts).

stages.name: Player's share of his team's first goal
stages.description: Conditional on Argentina scoring first at minute t, Messi must be on the pitch at t and be the scorer. His share comes from his non-penalty shot and xG share, his penalty duty (a first goal from the spot almost certainly belongs to the designated taker), direct free kicks, and the probability of an own goal by the opponent. A substitution plan for a veteran player reduces the share late in the match and in extra time.
stages.distribution: Time-varying share with a drop to zero after substitution; penalty route is a discrete jump in share; overall a small probability per match.

stages.name: Advancement conditional on leading first
stages.description: After scoring first, the team must advance. In knockouts a 1-0 lead converts often but the trailing side raises its attacking intensity, and an equaliser sends the match into a regulation-level state with extra time and penalties still available to either side. Earlier first goals leave more time for a response; stronger teams protect leads better.
stages.distribution: Conditional probability, typically high (around 0.75-0.9), decreasing in the time remaining and increasing in the strength gap.

stages.name: Joint integration of the legs
stages.description: The combo probability integrates, over the first-goal minute, the hazard that the named player scores first at that minute times the conditional advancement probability given the lead from that minute. A minute-level simulation that tracks score, substitutions and phase is the natural tool; validating the joint indicator against historical matches shows how far the dependence moves the result from a product of marginals.
stages.distribution: Joint Bernoulli with strong positive dependence between legs; dependence ratio typically well above 1 for a player on the stronger side.

stages.name: Leg parsing and settlement
stages.description: Each prepack names its legs in rules_primary only. For the sampled one, the first-goal window explicitly includes extra time, advancement implicitly includes a shootout, and own goals, DNP and postponement are not addressed. Other prepacks in the series may combine different legs, so a per-event parse is required before any probability is computed.
stages.distribution: Deterministic mapping from parsed flags; unparsed or ambiguous legs create discrete settlement risk.

soc.combo_leg_conditional_dependence.label: Conditional probability of each combo leg given the other legs
soc.combo_leg_conditional_dependence.mechanism: Legs of a same-match combo are generated by the same score path, so P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B | A) with P(B | A) often far from P(B).
soc.combo_leg_conditional_dependence.rationale: Pricing a prepack as a product of marginals is wrong in sign and size: a named player scoring first puts his team 1-0 up, which raises its advancement probability sharply, while legs such as 'opponent wins' would be strongly negatively dependent. The dependence also varies with when the first goal tends to arrive.
soc.combo_leg_conditional_dependence.measurement: Simulate the match minute by minute (team goal hazards by score state, player on-pitch indicator, ET and shootout) 50k times per fixture as of T-60; record joint indicators of each leg; dependence ratio = P(A and B) / (P(A) P(B)) and P(B | A); validate on historical matches by binning predicted P(B | A) against realised frequencies; no market prices used.
raw_data: goal events with minute and scorer
match results incl. ET and shootout
soc.combo_leg_conditional_dependence.why: The second leg's probability conditional on the first leg is the core of a two-leg prepack.

soc.lead_protection_knockout_conversion.label: Knockout advancement probability after scoring first, by minute and strength gap
soc.lead_protection_knockout_conversion.mechanism: In single-match knockouts the side that scores first advances most of the time, but the conversion depends on the minute of the goal, the strength gap and whether extra time and penalties remain as an escape route for the trailing side.
soc.lead_protection_knockout_conversion.rationale: This is the conditional advancement curve the Messi-scores-first leg feeds into. It differs from league win probability after scoring first because a trailing team that equalises can still win in extra time or on penalties, and favourites who lead protect differently than underdogs.
soc.lead_protection_knockout_conversion.measurement: From knockout matches since 2002 (World Cup, Euros, Copa America, UCL/UEL knockouts): for each match, minute of first goal (5-min buckets), pre-match rating gap (Elo difference deciles) and whether the first scorer advanced; fit logistic P(advance | first goal minute, gap, scoring side) with spline on minute; shrink tournament-specific effects to pooled with k=50.

interactions.mechanism: Both legs depend on the first-goal minute: an early goal by the player gives the opponent more time to equalise, a late one nearly secures advancement, so the joint probability is an integral over minute, not a product.
interactions.how_to_test: Simulate the joint with and without minute dependence and compare predicted joint frequencies with historical first-scorer-and-advance outcomes binned by first-goal minute.

interactions.mechanism: If the player's expected withdrawal minute precedes the typical first-goal minute in a low-scoring match, his scorer share collapses; above that threshold the scorer leg is insensitive to small changes in substitution timing.
interactions.how_to_test: Contrast realised first-scorer rates for players subbed before vs after 60' grouped by match total-goal expectation.

interactions.mechanism: The dependence ratio P(advance | first goal) / P(advance) shrinks as the player's team becomes a stronger favourite, because its unconditional advancement is already near one; underdog stars show the largest uplift.
interactions.how_to_test: Plot the empirical dependence ratio against pre-match Elo gap in knockout matches.

interactions.mechanism: VAR-era penalty awards raise the penalty share of first goals, and that share is credited to the designated taker, so a taker's scorer leg rises with the tournament's VAR penalty rate.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare designated-taker first-goal shares before and after VAR introduction at major tournaments.

interactions.mechanism: If the opponent equalises, advancement reverts to a near-even tie with extra time and penalties, so the response hazard matters only through the share of first-scorer paths that are later levelled.
interactions.how_to_test: Among knockout matches where the first scorer was equalised, measure the first scorer's eventual advancement rate against an even-tie baseline.

nonlinearities.shape: increasing S-curve in the minute of the first goal
nonlinearities.why: Advancement probability after scoring first rises slowly for early goals and steeply after about 70 minutes as the opponent runs out of time, then saturates near one.

nonlinearities.shape: piecewise: zero if DNP, linear in minutes on pitch otherwise
nonlinearities.why: The scorer leg requires being on the pitch; a DNP is a point mass at zero and partial minutes scale the share roughly in proportion to exposure.

catalog_entry.label: Soccer player appearance, squad selection and availability
catalog_entry.target: Whether a named player (or pair) is selected, named in a squad, or records playing time for a team in a match or window.
catalog_entry.mechanism: Appearance is a chain of gates rather than a performance: the player must be eligible (registered, under contract, eligible for the federation), fit on the match day, selected into the matchday squad, and then actually used by the coach, either from the start or as a substitute. Single-match contracts settle on official playing time in that game; window contracts are a union over every qualifying fixture before a deadline, with fitness persisting between matches; pair contracts require two players' on-pitch intervals to overlap. The probabilities are generated by injury recovery, contract and registration status, coach preference and rotation, and the number of qualifying fixtures.

mechanism.summary: Appearance outcomes are generated by sequential gates. Eligibility: the player must be registered for the team (contract signed, roster space, federation eligibility); for an out-of-contract player this can dominate. Fitness: a currently injured player's return date is a right-skewed distribution with setback risk, and fit players face a per-match hazard of new injury or suspension. Selection: given fitness, the coach decides matchday squad and XI from role, form, rotation and stakes. Usage: a bench player enters only if the coach substitutes him, which depends on score state and substitutions left. Single-match contracts are one pass through the gates; window contracts take the union over the qualifying fixtures with strong persistence of fitness and eligibility across matches; pair contracts need both players' on-pitch intervals to intersect, which depends on whether they are complements or rivals for one role.

stages.name: Eligibility and registration gate
stages.description: Before fitness or selection matter, the player must be eligible to appear for the named team: a current contract and league registration for club contracts (relevant to an NWSL player whose contract status is in question), and federation eligibility plus a call-up for national-team windows. Transfer windows, roster limits and negotiation progress make this a discrete state with a time-varying hazard of opening.
stages.distribution: Binary state with a hazard of switching to eligible; often a mass of probability on 'never within the window'.

stages.name: Fitness on each qualifying match day
stages.description: For an injured player, the probability of being fit by each date comes from the return-to-play distribution of the injury type, which has a long right tail from setbacks. For a fit player, a per-match hazard of fresh injury or suspension from card accumulation applies. Fitness states persist across consecutive matches, so window outcomes are strongly autocorrelated rather than independent per fixture.
stages.distribution: Right-skewed return time (log-normal-like) with a setback mixture; daily availability series with high persistence.

stages.name: Coach selection into matchday squad and XI
stages.description: Given fitness, the coach chooses the matchday squad and starting XI. Core starters are near-certain; fringe players depend on form, tactical fit and rotation. End-of-season or dead-rubber club matches and pre-tournament friendlies raise rotation and give minutes to fringe players while resting stars. Press conferences and confirmed lineups at T-60 update this stage sharply.
stages.distribution: Start probability per match close to 0 or 1 for most players with a mid-range mass for rotation candidates.

stages.name: Entry from the bench and minutes recorded
stages.description: A player on the bench records playing time only if brought on; the probability depends on position, the coach's substitution habits, the score state (comfortable leads and heavy deficits produce more changes) and remaining substitutions. For single-match contracts like the Messi game this is the main residual uncertainty after the lineup is known.
stages.distribution: Bernoulli entry given bench with probability varying by game state; entry minute right-skewed toward 60-85'.

stages.name: Window union and pair overlap
stages.description: Window contracts aggregate over every qualifying fixture before the deadline, so the fixture count and type matter as much as the per-match probability. The pair contract needs the two Real Madrid midfielders' on-pitch intervals to overlap in at least one official match in late May, which depends on their joint availability and on whether the coach uses them together or as alternatives in the same role.
stages.distribution: Union probability 1 - prod(1 - p_m) under positive dependence across matches; pair overlap is a joint distribution of two interval processes.

stages.name: Scope and settlement wording
stages.description: Each series defines participation differently: entering with official playing time, playing for a team within a window, simultaneous presence, or squad naming. Whether friendlies count is explicit only for the pair contract; minimum minutes are undefined for the window contracts. These flags must be stored per series and decide which fixtures enter the union.
stages.distribution: Deterministic given the flags; unresolved flags create two candidate fixture sets with different union probabilities.

soc.return_to_play_timeline.label: Injury return-to-play timeline for a named player
soc.return_to_play_timeline.mechanism: A currently injured player re-enters selection only after a recovery period whose length depends on injury type, severity, setbacks and the club's or federation's medical caution.
soc.return_to_play_timeline.rationale: Window contracts (play before a date) are dominated by whether the player is fit for any qualifying match before the deadline; the right object is the distribution of the return date, which is right-skewed with setback risk, not a point estimate from a press release.
soc.return_to_play_timeline.measurement: Per player at the as-of date: injury type and body part, date of injury, reported expected absence; map to a reference-class return-time distribution (median and quantiles by injury type and age from historical absence records, e.g. hamstring grade 2 median about 3-5 weeks); add setback probability per injury type; update daily with training-return reports; output P(available on date d) for every date in the window.
soc.return_to_play_timeline.why: Gives P(fit for each fixture in the window) for currently injured players such as a striker carrying a muscle injury.

soc.pair_onpitch_overlap_model.label: Joint on-pitch overlap probability for two named players
soc.pair_onpitch_overlap_model.mechanism: Two players are simultaneously on the pitch only if both are available and the coach uses them together, which depends on whether they are complements or substitutes for the same role.
soc.pair_onpitch_overlap_model.rationale: Marginal start probabilities miss positional competition: two midfielders who can each play the defensive midfield role may be rotated as alternatives, producing negative correlation, while two first-choice starters overlap almost surely when both are fit. The overlap is also helped by one starting and the other entering before the first leaves.
soc.pair_onpitch_overlap_model.measurement: From the club's lineups and substitution logs over the current and previous season under the same coach: for each match where both were available, indicator of any overlap interval > 0 minutes; logistic model on both players' availability, competition, rotation index and score state; output P(overlap in match m), then window P = 1 - product over matches of (1 - p_m) adjusted for injury persistence via shared availability draws.
soc.pair_onpitch_overlap_model.why: Settles KXRMAPLAYTOGETHER-type pair contracts that require simultaneous participation.

soc.window_qualifying_fixture_count.label: Number and type of qualifying matches inside the contract window
soc.window_qualifying_fixture_count.mechanism: Window contracts are a union over matches; the more qualifying fixtures (official vs friendly, club vs national team) fall inside the window, the more chances to appear.
soc.window_qualifying_fixture_count.rationale: Calendars differ by window: a national-team window may have only a few friendlies before a tournament, a club window at season end may include a final matchday with heavy rotation, and an NWSL window spans a full season. Whether friendlies count is often unstated, so the count must be carried per scope reading.
soc.window_qualifying_fixture_count.measurement: For the subject team and window [as-of, deadline]: list scheduled fixtures with competition, official/friendly flag and date; conditional fixtures (cup replays, playoffs) weighted by survival probability; output counts under each scope reading (official only; including friendlies); refreshed when fixtures are added or moved.
soc.window_qualifying_fixture_count.why: Converts per-match appearance probability into a window probability.

soc.registration_and_league_eligibility.label: Registration, contract and league eligibility to play for the named team
soc.registration_and_league_eligibility.mechanism: A player can appear for a team only if registered with it under the league's or federation's rules; this depends on contract status, transfer windows, roster limits and national-team eligibility.
soc.registration_and_league_eligibility.rationale: For contracts like 'plays for any NWSL team before a date' or 'plays for the national team before a date', the binding constraint can be off-field: an expired contract, an unfinished move abroad, a roster-registration deadline, or a federation switch. These are discrete states with their own hazards.
soc.registration_and_league_eligibility.measurement: Per player at the as-of date: current club and contract end date, free-agent flag, league registration windows and roster limits for the target league, reported negotiation stage {none, talks, agreed}, national-team eligibility state (caps, federation switch status); map each state to a hazard of becoming eligible by date d using base rates of similar cases; timestamp every news item.
soc.registration_and_league_eligibility.why: Can make the appearance impossible regardless of fitness or coach preference.

catalog_entry.label: Soccer squad selection and starting lineup
catalog_entry.target: A named player is included in a national team's officially announced final tournament squad, or in the starting XI at kickoff of a match.
catalog_entry.mechanism: Both contracts settle on a coach's list, not on play. A final World Cup squad is a fixed-size list drawn from a candidate pool by a coach who relies heavily on players he has repeatedly called up, subject to de facto positional quotas, the player's fitness at the deadline and, for veterans, the player's own decision to take part; late injury replacements before the first match add a path for reserves. A starting XI is the coach's match-specific choice given the opponent, fitness, suspensions and the stakes of the match, and is settled by who is on the field at kickoff.

Rotation is concentrated in matches with low stakes for the coach, such as a clinched third group match or the third-place match, which flips starter probabilities for squad players.
For veterans with long call-up histories, inclusion hinges almost entirely on stated intent and fitness rather than on competition.

mechanism.summary: Final-squad inclusion is a constrained ranking. The coach has a fixed number of slots with positional quotas and fills them mostly from players he has called up and used in recent windows; candidates outside that core enter mainly when a rival is injured or out of form. Fitness at the list deadline removes some favoured candidates, and late injury replacements before the first match give reserves a second path. For veteran stars the coach's choice is near-automatic, so the outcome turns on the player's intent and fitness. Starting-XI inclusion is a match-level choice: core starters are fixed when fit, while squad players start when stakes are low (dead rubbers, third-place match), when a starter is suspended for card accumulation, or when the coach changes system for an opponent. Leaks and press conferences resolve much of the uncertainty before official release.

stages.name: Candidate pool and coach familiarity
stages.description: The relevant pool is players the coach has called up in recent international windows, weighted by recency and minutes. Coaches rarely add uncapped or long-absent players to a final list, so the call-up record under the current coach dominates club form or market value. A coaching change before the tournament resets this pool and widens uncertainty.
stages.distribution: Highly bimodal: core players near 0.95+, fringe candidates spread over 0.1-0.6, outsiders near zero.

stages.name: Positional quotas and rival competition
stages.description: Slots are allocated by position, so a candidate competes with direct rivals: three goalkeepers, a fixed number of full-backs and centre-backs, and so on. Versatile players can occupy two queues. Rival injuries or form changes shift a fringe candidate's chance without any change in his own status, making the outcome correlated across candidates of the same position.
stages.distribution: Negative dependence among candidates for the same position (sum of inclusions fixed by the quota).

stages.name: Fitness, intent and the replacement window
stages.description: At the deadline a favoured candidate can be excluded by injury; veterans can self-select out. After the list, injured players may be replaced until shortly before the first match, and under KXWCSQUAD both the withdrawn player and the replacement settle YES. This creates asymmetric paths: injuries cost favoured players only before the list but help reserves afterwards.
stages.distribution: Discrete injury shocks with timing relative to the deadline; replacement probability small but concentrated on the first reserve per position.

stages.name: Match-day starting XI decision
stages.description: For a starting-XI contract the coach chooses eleven given the opponent, system, fitness, card suspensions and stakes. Core starters are near-certain when fit; others depend on rotation, which is heavy in matches with little at stake such as the third-place play-off or a group finale after qualification. Press-conference hints and confirmed lineups at T-60 nearly settle the question; the residual is a warm-up withdrawal.
stages.distribution: Per-player start probability with a large mass near 0 and 1; announced-XI to kickoff changes are rare (well under 1%).

stages.name: Information release and settlement
stages.description: Official lists and lineups arrive at known times, preceded by leaks of varying reliability. Settlement uses the final list (provisional lists excluded) or the XI on the field at kickoff, and a match not played by the stated date resolves NO for the starting-XI series. Correct timing of each information release is essential to avoid look-ahead in back-tests.
stages.distribution: Step changes in probability at leak and announcement times; deterministic settlement thereafter.

soc.national_team_call_up_history.label: Call-up, caps and minutes under the current national-team coach
soc.national_team_call_up_history.mechanism: National coaches pick final squads mostly from players they have repeatedly called up and used; a candidate's selection record in recent camps is the strongest single predictor of final-squad inclusion.
soc.national_team_call_up_history.rationale: Club form and market value matter much less than coach familiarity: players absent from the last several camps are rarely added to a final list, while ever-present players are dropped mainly for injury. The input must be measured under the current coach because a new coach resets the pool.
soc.national_team_call_up_history.measurement: Per candidate at the as-of date: number of camps called up and matches started/minutes in the last 6 international windows under the current coach (weight w=0.7^k for window k back), caps, and whether named in the latest provisional list; shrink coach-specific rates to the federation's historical retention rate with k=4 windows.
soc.national_team_call_up_history.why: Best predictor of whether a candidate is on the final World Cup squad list.

soc.positional_slot_competition.label: Positional slot competition and quota for the final squad
soc.positional_slot_competition.mechanism: A final squad has a fixed number of slots with de facto positional quotas (three goalkeepers, two per full-back side, etc.), so inclusion is a ranking among direct rivals for those slots.
soc.positional_slot_competition.rationale: Selection is zero-sum within a position: a rival's injury or form surge changes a candidate's chance without any change in the candidate. Versatile players who cover two positions gain value in a squad of fixed size.
soc.positional_slot_competition.measurement: Per federation: candidate pool by primary/secondary position; expected slots per position from the coach's past squads (mean and spread); rank candidates within position by a selection score combining call-up history, minutes and fitness; compute P(rank within quota) by simulation over rival injury and form draws; versatility flag adds the candidate to two queues.
raw_data: past final squads of the coach by position
soc.positional_slot_competition.why: Turns a candidate's standing into a probability of occupying one of the limited squad slots.

soc.squad_list_deadline_and_replacement_.label: Squad-list deadlines, size and late-replacement rules
soc.squad_list_deadline_and_replacement_.mechanism: Tournament regulations set the provisional and final list dates, squad size and conditions under which a named player may be replaced, all of which change what counts as final for settlement.
soc.squad_list_deadline_and_replacement_.rationale: KXWCSQUAD counts players added after the initial announcement but before the team's first match, and keeps a withdrawn player as YES. The replacement window therefore adds YES paths for reserves; the squad size fixes the number of YES outcomes per federation.
soc.squad_list_deadline_and_replacement_.measurement: From FIFA tournament regulations: provisional list date and size, final list deadline, squad size, replacement conditions (serious injury/illness certified, until 24 h before first match or as specified); map onto each contract's own rule (added before first match counts; withdrawals stay YES); store version-hashed.
soc.squad_list_deadline_and_replacement_.why: Defines the YES set and the extra replacement path for reserves.

soc.squad_announcement_leak_reports.label: Pre-announcement reports of squad lists and starting XIs
soc.squad_announcement_leak_reports.mechanism: Journalists and federation sources often report squad lists or lineups hours to days before official release, with reliability varying by source.
soc.squad_announcement_leak_reports.rationale: Squad and XI decisions are made before they are announced; credible leaks move the probability close to 0 or 1 ahead of the official list. Source tiering is essential because speculative lists are common.
soc.squad_announcement_leak_reports.measurement: Event log of reports with timestamp, source tier (federation/official, established national-team beat reporter, aggregator), content (player in/out, starter/bench); estimate P(correct | tier) from past tournaments' lists and XIs; combine via log-odds updating with tier weights, capped to avoid overconfidence from correlated sources.
soc.squad_announcement_leak_reports.why: Updates squad and XI probabilities before the official announcement.

soc.player_tournament_participation_inte.label: Player's stated intent to take part (retirement, availability declarations)
soc.player_tournament_participation_inte.mechanism: Veteran stars can self-select out through retirement or by declaring themselves unavailable, and late-career players sometimes signal intent long before the squad is named.
soc.player_tournament_participation_inte.rationale: For marquee veterans the coach's choice is close to automatic if the player wants to go; the residual risk is the player's decision and his late-season fitness, not competition for the slot.
soc.player_tournament_participation_inte.measurement: Per candidate: dated statements of intent (retired from national team, 'will be available', undecided) classified into three states, with time decay; base rates of veterans who declared availability and then were named; combine with fitness status at the deadline.
soc.player_tournament_participation_inte.why: Key residual risk for veteran-star squad contracts.

catalog_entry.label: Team consecutive-win streak
catalog_entry.target: Whether a team strings together at least N consecutive wins across all competitions within a stated period.
catalog_entry.mechanism: The contract settles YES if somewhere in the calendar year the team wins at least N matches in a row across all competitions. The outcome is generated by an ordered sequence of match win probabilities (each well below one, with draws as frequent streak-breakers), the number of matches available before the year ends, and serial dependence from form, injuries and manager changes that makes good and bad runs cluster. The probability of a run of length N is a highly convex function of the typical per-match win probability, so modest changes in team strength or schedule order move it a lot; once the run is achieved the contract is settled.

inputs.why: Per-match win probabilities in order are the core input to a run-length calculation.
Serial correlation of results makes streaks likelier than an independent-match calculation suggests.
Opponent-adjusted strength sets each match's win probability.
Uncertainty in team strength is shared across all matches and fattens the tails of the streak outcome.
Draws break a win streak; a draw-prone team has fewer streaks for the same points rate.
Venue ordering in the sequence changes which windows are winnable.
A manager change shifts strength and often produces a short-term run, a regime switch for the streak.
Key-player absences lower win probability over a block of consecutive fixtures.
Cup survival adds fixtures (often winnable early rounds) and congestion.
Which competitions count and whether a shootout win counts as a win.
Season points distribution is the blueprint's target; checked here for relevance.
Rules define the calendar window and all-competitions scope.
As-of run length and absorbing YES state.
Ordered fixtures across two seasons.
Summer change in strength for the autumn half.

interactions.hypothesis: Positive serial dependence raises the streak probability most for mid-table teams whose per-match win probability is near 0.5, where independent runs of five are rare.
Clusters of home matches against weaker opponents create windows where a run is plausible; the same fixtures spread out yield fewer runs.
A manager change or summer rebuild resets the strength regime for all later matches at once, so the streak probability depends on a shared latent shift.

contract.settlement_definition: KXWINSTREAKMANU-27-5 settles YES if Manchester United win at least 5 games in a row across all competitions in the year 2026 (strike type 'greater', floor 4.5, so 5+). Consecutive means without a non-win in between in counted competitions. Whether a win on penalties counts as a win, whether friendlies count, whether a run that begins in late 2025 counts, and the source of truth are not stated; the ticker suffix '27' differs from the 2026 window in the rules text.

rules_evidence.quote: If Manchester United win at least 5 games in a row across all competitions in the year 2026, then the market resolves to Yes.
rules_evidence.establishes: Threshold of 5 consecutive wins, all competitions, calendar year 2026.

rules_evidence.quote: Will Manchester United men's soccer win at least 5 games in a row this year?
rules_evidence.establishes: Title confirms the men's team and an 'at least N' strike.

variants_and_edge_cases: Shootout outcomes: a cup tie drawn after extra time and won on penalties is a draw in most statistical records; whether it continues or breaks the streak is not stated.
Friendlies: 'all competitions' normally excludes pre-season friendlies, but the rules do not say so; a July 2026 friendly tour could add or break wins under a broad reading.
Window boundary: a run spanning Dec 2025 into Jan 2026 may need all five wins inside 2026; the rules imply wins 'in the year 2026' but do not say how straddling runs are treated.
Other strikes (e.g. 3+, 4+, 6+) may exist as a ladder; nested strikes must give a monotone probability curve.
The ticker ends in '27' while rules say 2026; the event window could be mislabelled or the series rolled over.
contract.settlement_data_source: Not stated; presumably official competition results as reported by Kalshi's provider.

mechanism.summary: A win streak of at least five in a calendar year is a run-length event over an ordered sequence of matches. Each match has a win probability that depends on opponent strength, venue, lineup and congestion; for a club of Manchester United's recent level, many league matches carry win probabilities around 0.4-0.6, and draws are frequent streak-breakers. The number of matches remaining in the window caps chances, and the order matters because runs need consecutive winnable fixtures. Results are not independent: form, injuries, a manager change or a summer rebuild move strength over blocks of matches, which clusters wins and raises the run probability above an independent calculation. Finally, the contract's scope rules (competitions counted, penalty wins, window boundaries) define the sequence, and the run state at the as-of date sets how far the team is from the threshold or whether it is already met.

stages.name: Per-match win probability
stages.description: Each counted match's win probability comes from opponent-adjusted strength, venue, lineup strength and draw propensity. For a mid-to-upper Premier League side, home matches against bottom-half opponents may approach 0.65, away matches at top sides 0.2-0.3. Draws, not only losses, end a streak, so a draw-heavy style lowers the run probability for the same points per game.
stages.distribution: Vector of probabilities with heterogeneity across matches; each match a three-outcome event where only the win continues the run.

stages.name: Ordered sequence and opportunity count
stages.description: The calendar year 2026 spans the second half of 2025-26 and the first half of 2026-27, with a summer break that includes the World Cup. The ordered fixture list, conditional cup ties and European matches (if qualified) define how many windows of five consecutive matches exist and how winnable each is. Cup survival adds fixtures but also congestion.
stages.distribution: Discrete count of matches (roughly 35-50) with a stochastic component from cup progression.

stages.name: Serial dependence and regime changes
stages.description: Results cluster because the team's true strength drifts and because blocks of matches share lineup and fitness conditions. A manager change often brings a temporary bounce, and the summer transfer window can reset strength for the autumn. These shared shifts make streaks likelier than independent trials and widen uncertainty about the run outcome.
stages.distribution: Latent AR(1)-like strength process with occasional jumps (manager change, summer reset).

stages.name: Run-length probability from the current state
stages.description: Given the run state at the as-of date, the probability of reaching five consecutive wins before the window closes is computed by a Markov chain on run length over the ordered match probabilities, integrated over the latent strength path. The response is strongly convex in per-match win probability: P(at least one run of 5 in 20 matches) is about 0.10 at p=0.4 and about 0.36 at p=0.55 under independence.
stages.distribution: Probability bounded in [0,1], convex in typical p, absorbing once the run is achieved.

stages.name: Scope and settlement
stages.description: The rules count all competitions in calendar 2026 but do not address penalty-shootout outcomes, friendlies, or runs straddling the year boundary, and the ticker suffix differs from the stated year. Each reading defines a different sequence, so scope flags must be recorded per reading and the streak computed under each.
stages.distribution: Deterministic given the flags; disagreement between readings matters mainly when a cup shootout or friendly falls inside a candidate run.

soc.current_win_run_state.label: Current consecutive-win run and threshold status at the as-of date
soc.current_win_run_state.mechanism: A streak contract is path dependent: the probability of reaching N consecutive wins depends on how many consecutive wins the team already has and whether the threshold has already been reached inside the window.
soc.current_win_run_state.rationale: Once five straight wins occur in the window the contract is settled YES (absorbing state); before that, a team on a three-win run needs only two more, so the as-of run length changes the probability far more than any rating change. Runs that started before the window boundary may or may not count.
soc.current_win_run_state.measurement: At the as-of timestamp: number of consecutive wins in all counted competitions ending at the latest completed match, split into wins inside and before the window start; max run achieved inside the window so far; indicator threshold_reached; applied rule for wins on penalties per the scope flags; recomputed after each match.
raw_data: match date, competition, result incl. ET/penalty outcome
soc.current_win_run_state.why: Sets the starting state of the run-length calculation and detects early settlement.

soc.calendar_year_fixture_sequence.label: Ordered fixture sequence across a calendar year spanning two seasons
soc.calendar_year_fixture_sequence.mechanism: A calendar-year window crosses the end of one season and the start of the next, with a summer gap, a World Cup in 2026, and cup fixtures whose existence depends on survival.
soc.calendar_year_fixture_sequence.rationale: Streaks need consecutive wins in an ordered list, so the order of hard and easy fixtures matters: five winnable matches in a row are far likelier to produce a streak than the same matches split by away games at top sides. The number of remaining matches before the window ends also caps the chances.
soc.calendar_year_fixture_sequence.measurement: Ordered list of all fixtures from as-of to Dec 31 in counted competitions with date, venue, opponent and competition; conditional cup/European fixtures included with survival probabilities; summer friendlies tagged separately; the sequence is refreshed when fixtures are rescheduled for television or cup ties.
free_sources: Premier League and FA fixture lists
raw_data: fixture list with dates and venues
soc.calendar_year_fixture_sequence.why: Provides the ordered opportunities over which a run of N wins can form.

soc.season_boundary_strength_reset.label: Strength change across the summer between seasons
soc.season_boundary_strength_reset.mechanism: Squad turnover, transfers, a new manager or tactical change over the summer can move team strength materially between the spring and autumn halves of a calendar-year window.
soc.season_boundary_strength_reset.rationale: A single rating applied to the whole year misstates the autumn win probabilities; the uncertainty about the reset is large at the as-of date and is shared across all autumn matches, which widens the streak probability's dependence on one latent variable.
soc.season_boundary_strength_reset.measurement: Per club: change in pre-season rating relative to end-of-season rating in each of the last 10 summers (from Elo or xG ratings), regressed on net transfer spend relative to squad value, manager change and departures of top-minute players; forecast distribution of the summer shift as of the as-of date, sd shrunk to the league-wide sd of summer shifts.
soc.season_boundary_strength_reset.why: Shifts all autumn-match win probabilities together.
